extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent applications for subject-matter eligibility (35 U.S.C. 101) including how to identify judicial exceptions, support rejections, evaluate applicant responses, and for assessing compliance with the utility requirement (35 U.S.C. 101 and 112(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence requirement for finding judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: At Step 2A Prong Two or Step 2B, there is no requirement for evidence to support a finding that the exception is not integrated into a practical application or that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more than the exception unless the examiner asserts that additional limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities in Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may identify an abstract idea (or other judicial exception) without relying on external evidence; however, if the examiner asserts additional elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional, then the examiner must support that assertion as set forth in the MPEP (see following criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support required before asserting 'well-understood, routine, conventional'
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should not assert that an additional element (or combination of elements) is well-understood, routine, or conventional unless the examiner finds, and expressly supports the rejection in writing with one or more of the following:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible supports: (A) citation to an express statement in the specification or to an applicant's prosecution statement demonstrating the element is well-understood/routine/conventional; (B) citation to one or more court decisions discussed in MPEP § 2106.05(d) noting the conventional nature; (C) citation to a publication demonstrating the element's well-understood, routine, conventional nature; (D) a statement that the examiner is taking official notice, used only where the examiner's personal knowledge clearly establishes widespread prevalence or common use. The examiner must ensure the record shows the basis (see MPEP for specifics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification cannot be silent basis for conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding that an element is well-understood, routine, or conventional cannot be based only on the fact that the specification is silent with respect to describing such element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification can demonstrate conventionality only when it explicitly describes the additional elements as well-understood, routine, conventional, commercially available, or indicates that particulars are sufficiently well-known that the specification need not describe them to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Silence alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of court decisions to support conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should be careful to ensure the claim limitations before the examiner are the same as those found to be well-understood, routine, conventional by the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The additional elements under examination should be recited in the same manner (same high level of generality) as in those court decisions; similarity is not enough. Court decisions do not imply that all computer functions are conventional or that a generic computer performing generic functions is necessarily ineligible. See DDR Holdings and MPEP § 2106.05(f) for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publications as evidence of conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: A citation to a publication that demonstrates the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate publications include books, manuals, review articles, or other state-of-the-art sources that show wide prevalence or common use. A single patent or published application is generally insufficient to establish that an element is well-understood, routine, conventional unless it demonstrably shows wide prevalence. Distinguish between 'printed publication' for 102 and evidence of 'well-known, routine, conventional'—they are separate inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official notice for conventionality (limited use)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement that the examiner is taking official notice of the well-understood, routine, conventional nature of the additional element(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use official notice only when examiner is certain based on personal knowledge that the element is widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field (comparable to elements so well-known they need not be described to satisfy 35 U.S.C.112(a)). Example: taking official notice that a generic computer component using the Internet to gather data is well-understood. Follow procedures in MPEP § 2144.03 and be prepared to address applicant challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraphs required for eligibility rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specified form paragraphs for 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections depending on the step and the nature of the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraphs 7.04.01, 7.05, and 7.05.01 for rejections based on failure to claim a statutory category (Step 1). Use form paragraphs 7.04.01, 7.05, and 7.05.016 for rejections based on being directed to a judicial exception without providing an inventive concept (Step 2B). If the judicial exception is a 'tentative abstract idea', also include form paragraph 7.05.017 and obtain TC Director signature.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.04.01 — Statement of Statutory Basis (35 U.S.C. 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 7.04.01 includes the text of 35 U.S.C. 101 and must precede the first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in all first actions on the merits and final rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner Note: This paragraph must precede first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in first actions and final rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.05.01 — Nonstatutory (Not One of Four Statutory Categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use where the claimed invention is directed to nonstatutory subject matter (does not fall within a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bracket 1, explain why the claimed invention is not patent eligible by identifying what the claim is directed to (e.g., signal per se, mere information/data, contract, human being) and explain why it does not fall within the statutory categories. Precede with 7.05 and follow MPEP § 2106 guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.05.016 — Nonstatutory (Directed to a Judicial Exception without Inventive Concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph to explain that the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception without significantly more and to identify and explain the exception and why additional elements fail to amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Populate brackets: (1) identify whether claim directed to law of nature, natural phenomenon (including product of nature), or abstract idea; (2) identify the exception as recited in the claim and explain why it is an exception (e.g., map to abstract idea groupings in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2)); (3) explain why the combination of additional elements fails to integrate the exception into a practical application; (4) identify additional elements and explain why, separately and in combination, they do not add significantly more (inventive concept). Provide examples (e.g., generic computer elements merely implement idea on a computer; data-gathering steps are extra-solution activity; placing a product of nature in a test tube is nominal).

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶ 7.05.017 — TC Director Approval for 'Tentative Abstract Idea'
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph requiring TC Director approval/signature when treating a 'tentative abstract idea'—a limitation not falling within the enumerated abstract idea groupings—as an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bracket 1, justify why the limitation is being treated as an abstract idea (e.g., among 'basic tools of scientific and technological work'). Insert TC Director signature in bracket 2. Use this paragraph in addition to 7.05.016 and obtain required approval per MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and options for applicant responding to eligibility rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: After examiner identifies why a claim is directed to an abstract idea, natural phenomenon, or law of nature without significantly more, the burden shifts to the applicant to either amend the claim, present persuasive arguments, and/or submit evidence (per MPEP § 716.01 and 37 CFR 1.132).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may: (i) amend claims to add/modify elements so claim amounts to significantly more or integrates into a practical application; (ii) present persuasive arguments why rejection is in error; (iii) submit evidence traversing rejection. Examiner must carefully consider all arguments and evidence and, if claims amended, determine broadest reasonable interpretation and repeat eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating whether additional elements integrate an exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more, consider the additional elements both individually and in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An additional element may, by itself, meaningfully limit the judicial exception (e.g., improve another technology or functioning of a computer) and thus integrate or amount to significantly more. Elements that are generic when considered individually may, in combination, perform non-generic functions and be sufficient (e.g., generic computer components in combination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner rebuttal and explanation where rejection maintained
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant properly challenges the examiner's findings but the examiner maintains the rejection, a rebuttal must be provided in the next Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate rebuttal examples: (1) explain why the abstract idea identified is similar to the concept in a cited case if applicant's challenge to tentative abstract idea not persuasive; (2) if applicant rebuts assertion of conventionality, reevaluate and consider providing supporting evidence or affidavit/declaration (37 CFR 1.104(d)(2)) if official notice was taken; (3) where applicant amends to add generic computer/components claiming 'specially programmed' machine, analyze whether elements integrate exception—mere addition of generic computer is insufficient (see Alice); (4) if applicant argues lack of preemption/specificity, reconsider Step 2A (is claim improvement to computer or other technology?) and then Step 2B to evaluate inventive concept in combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarifying the record when claims are found eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims are deemed patent eligible, the examiner may make clarifying remarks on the record (e.g., reference the specification describing the claimed improvement and note claim elements producing that improvement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifying remarks may be made at any point during prosecution or with a notice of allowance and help explain rationale for a rejection or BRI of a claim (example: carrier wave interpretation for a computer-readable-medium claim). Use to assist applicant understanding and response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility examination — initial steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel shall read the claims and the supporting written description to determine what the applicant has claimed, noting any specific embodiments, and ensure the claims define statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If at any time it is readily apparent that the claimed invention has a well-established utility, do not impose a rejection based on lack of utility. Ensure claims are process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or improvement thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and test for 'well-established utility'
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention has a well-established utility if (i) a person of ordinary skill in the art would immediately appreciate why the invention is useful based on the characteristics of the invention, and (ii) the utility is specific, substantial, and credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these conditions are met, do not impose a rejection for lack of utility. 'Immediately appreciate' is judged from perspective of one of ordinary skill in the art in view of disclosure and any other evidence of record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific and substantial utility requirement and credibility assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention must have a specific and substantial utility; credibility is assessed from perspective of one of ordinary skill in the art in view of the disclosure and any other evidence of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude 'throw-away', 'insubstantial', or 'nonspecific' utilities (e.g., using a complex invention as landfill). Applicant need only provide one credible assertion of specific and substantial utility for each claimed invention. Credibility may be supported by test data, affidavits/declarations, patents, or printed publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to reject for lack of utility and associated 112(a) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If no assertion of specific and substantial utility made by applicant is credible, and the claimed invention does not have a readily apparent well-established utility, reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 for lack of utility and under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112 first paragraph) for failing to teach how to use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejecting under both statutes shifts burden to applicant to: (i) explicitly identify a specific and substantial utility; and (ii) provide evidence that one of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized that the identified specific and substantial utility was well-established at filing. Examiner should ensure adequate nexus between submitted evidence and properties of the claimed subject matter as disclosed in the application as filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing requirements for lack of specific/substantial/credible utility
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie showing of no specific and substantial utility or no specific and substantial credible utility must meet detailed elements before a rejection can be maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For asserted utility that is not specific/substantial: (i) provide an explanation setting forth reasoning; (ii) provide support for factual findings relied upon; (iii) evaluate all relevant evidence of record (including closest prior art). For asserted specific/substantial utility that is not credible: (i) explanation of why not credible; (ii) factual support; (iii) evaluation of all evidence. Where no specific and substantial utility is disclosed, prima facie showing need only establish applicant has not asserted a utility and no known well-established utility exists on record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation and evidence for utility rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rejection based on lack of utility should include a detailed explanation why the claimed invention has no specific and substantial credible utility and, whenever possible, documentary evidence to support the factual basis for the prima facie showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentary evidence can include scientific/technical journals, treatises, books, or U.S./foreign patents. If documentary evidence is unavailable, the examiner should explain the scientific basis for factual conclusions. The examiner must evaluate all relevant evidence of record when considering applicant responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of applicant factual statements and expert opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must treat as true a statement of fact made by an applicant in relation to an asserted utility, unless countervailing evidence shows a person of ordinary skill would have legitimate basis to doubt credibility; likewise accept qualified expert opinions based on relevant facts unless accuracy of those facts is questioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not disregard applicant factual statements solely because of disagreement over significance or meaning. Once a prima facie showing of no specific/substantial/credible utility has been properly established, the applicant bears the burden of rebuttal via amendment, reasoning, or evidence (e.g., declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 or printed publications). If applicant rebuts satisfactorily, withdraw corresponding 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112 rejections.
